props.title: Get Real
props.initialSlug: Gay teen navigates first love in 90s Britain

sections.content: Get Real (1998) stands as a landmark coming-of-age LGBTQ+ film from late 90s British cinema, arriving at a crucial moment when queer teen stories were rarely told with such honesty. Director Simon Shore crafted an intimate portrait of 16-year-old Steven Carter's journey of self-discovery that shares DNA with Beautiful Thing (1996) but carves its own distinct path. The film's treatment of first love between Steven and popular athlete John Dixon avoided the tragic endings common to earlier gay cinema, instead offering a nuanced look at teenage romance in a hostile environment.

sections.content: The late 1990s marked a shift in LGBTQ+ teen representation, with Get Real joining films like Show Me Love (1998) and Edge of Seventeen (1998) in portraying young queer characters with depth and authenticity rather than as tragic figures or comedic stereotypes. These films shared a common thread of examining the intersection of teenage social hierarchies with emerging queer identity, while grounding their stories in realistic family dynamics and school environments.

Get Real particularly excels in its handling of the complexities around coming out in a school environment, predating similar themes in later films like But I'm a Cheerleader (1999) and Summer Storm (2004). The film's use of Steven's school newspaper column as a vehicle for self-expression pioneered narrative devices that would become common in later LGBTQ+ teen films. sections.content: The success of Get Real helped pave the way for a new wave of British LGBTQ+ films including Wilde (1997) and later Pride (2014). Its realistic portrayal of suburban British life and school culture influenced later works like Handsome Devil (2016) and Dating Amber (2020), while its sensitive handling of coming out narratives set a template that continues to influence contemporary filmmakers.
